newsitem.title: MAURITIUS: Mauritian minister urges sugar mills to modernise.
newsitem.headline: Mauritian minister urges sugar mills to modernise.

text.p: Mauritian Agricultural Minister Arvin Boolell wants sugar mills on the Indian Ocean island to continue modernising and lower production costs so as to increase their competitive edge in the global sugar market.
Boolell told Reuters in an interview a consolidation programme for the factories would give the industry the added benefit of economies of scale in sugar production.

"In order to increase our competitiveness on the world markets, the sugar industry is condemned to modernisation and centralisation of its 17 factories. Mechanisation of field tasks should be implemented to lower output costs," he said.
"A consolidation policy will be implemented as it is seen as essential for the future of sugar industry," he added, referring to a government policy paper expected in coming months.
Boolell said in preparing the paper, he had met all the parties directly concerned and received written submissions from them.
"These papers spell out their concerns and the guarantees they wish to obtain from the government," he said.

Mauritius Sugar Producers' Association Director Patrick D'Arifat told Reuters in September he expected the centralisation of sugar mills would reduce the number of production units to 13 or 14 by the year 2000 from the present 17.

D'Arifat said the rationalisation process would have to address the issues of investment in sugar mills, compensation to workers at factories that were to be shut down and extra transport costs for small planters who would have to sell their products to other factories.
Boolell urged mills to diversify their activities into electric power production using bagasse, the cane by-product left after sugar syrup has been extracted.
A senior official at the Mauritius Sugar Authority (MSA) said 10 sugar factories would soon enter into agreements to sell power to the national Central Electricity Board (CEB).
Seven of the factories would produce electricity during the harvest season and three throughout the year.
"All new installations are being subjected to environment impact assessment studies," the MSA official said.
In the year 2001, when all electric power projects were up and running in the sugar mills, it was expected that the industry would meet 40 percent of the island's electricity demand.

Industry officials say Mauritius has an annual sugar production capacity of 650,000 tonnes. A guaranteed quota of around 510,000 tonnes is exported to the European Union every year under the Sugar Protocol of the Lome Convention at preferential prices which are higher than world market prices.
The Protocol will outlive the Convention, which expires in the year 2000, but while the export quota will remain, preferential prices will no longer be guaranteed.
With the prospect of lower export prices in the future, sugar mills in Mauritius are investing in modernisation programmes to boost their productivity and improve their competitive edge.
"Our policy is to achieve cost reduction, modernisation of factory equipment, optimisation of bagasse (use) and compliance with international accepted environment norms," Boolell said.
